title: Internal Energy
short_intro: Internal energy is the total microscopic energy of a system comprising the kinetic and potential energies of its constituent molecules, atoms, or subatomic particles. It is a state function representing an extensive property of thermodynamic systems.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of internal energy, its state function nature, dependence on temperature for ideal gases, and relation to the First Law of Thermodynamics.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Statistical interpretation via degrees of freedom, Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution, internal energy of real gases using van der Waals forces, and configurational internal energy.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
Degrees of Freedom and Law of Equipartition of Energy

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Basis of Internal Energy
bullets: Internal energy (U) includes translational, rotational, and vibrational kinetic energies of molecules, along with intermolecular potential energy.
It excludes macroscopic kinetic energy of the system as a whole and potential energy arising from external gravitational or electrostatic fields.
For an ideal gas, intermolecular forces are assumed zero, implying internal energy depends exclusively on temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Internal Energy as a State Function
bullets: U is a thermodynamic state function; its change dU between two equilibrium states depends only on the initial and final states, not the path.
Cyclic integrals of internal energy changes are identically zero: oint dU = 0.
Exact differential property allows dU to be integrated directly without path specification.

concept_notes.heading: Equpartition of Energy and Internal Energy
bullets: Each active degree of freedom contributes (1/2)k_BT per molecule or (1/2)RT per mole to the internal energy.
Monatomic gases possess 3 translational degrees of freedom, diatomic gases possess 5 (at room temperature) or 7 (at high temperature) degrees of freedom.
Total internal energy for an ideal gas is given by U = f/2 n RT where f is the total degrees of freedom.

concept_notes.heading: Internal Energy of Real Gases
bullets: Real gases possess intermolecular attractive and repulsive potentials, making internal energy a function of both temperature and volume (U = U(T, V)).
Joule's free expansion experiment shows that for a real gas, internal energy varies slightly with volume due to internal work against attractive forces.
Van der Waals correction introduces a potential energy term proportional to the square of density: U_{real} = (f/2)nRT - (a n^2 / V).

derivations.title: Internal Energy of an Ideal Gas using Law of Equipartition
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas in thermal equilibrium with f degrees of freedom
steps: State the mean energy associated with a single degree of freedom per molecule as (1/2)k_BT based on Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
Multiply the energy per degree of freedom by the number of degrees of freedom f to get total energy per molecule: E = (f/2)k_BT.
Scale up to N molecules (or n moles) by multiplying by Avogadro number N_A, yielding U = (f/2)N k_BT = (f/2)n RT.

derivations.title: Relation between Internal Energy Change and Heat Capacity
derivations.conditions: Constant volume process (isochoric process) for any pure substance
steps: Write the First Law of Thermodynamics: dQ = dU + dW, where dW = P dV.
For a constant volume process, dV = 0, so dW = 0, leading to dQ = dU.
Express molar heat capacity at constant volume as C_v = (1/n)(dQ/dT)_V.
Substitute dQ = dU to obtain dU = n C_v dT, and integrate for finite temperature changes.
derivations.result: Delta U = int_{T_1}^{T_2} n C_v dT

graphs_and_experiments.title: Internal Energy vs Temperature for an Ideal Gas
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a U vs T plot, where the slope represents (f/2)nR.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows direct proportionality between internal energy and absolute temperature for an ideal gas.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test understanding of linear dependence and identification of slopes for different gases (monatomic vs diatomic).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Joule's Free Expansion Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two insulated bulbs connected by a closed valve; one filled with gas, the other evacuated, submerged in a water bath.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: When the valve opens, gas expands into vacuum (dW = 0, dQ = 0), and temperature change is measured to test internal energy dependence on volume.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Demonstrates that internal energy of an ideal gas is independent of volume ((partial U / partial V)_T = 0).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Isothermal vs Adiabatic Curves on P-V Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two curves on a P-V plane starting from the same point, with the adiabatic curve steeper than the isothermal curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: In an adiabatic expansion, work is done at the expense of internal energy, leading to a drop in temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in calculations involving internal energy change during adiabatic processes (Delta U = -W).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the change in internal energy of 2 moles of a monoatomic ideal gas when its temperature is increased from 200 K to 300 K. (Given R = 8.314 J/(mol K))
solution_steps: Identify the gas type: Monoatomic gas has 3 degrees of freedom (f = 3).
Write the formula for internal energy change: Delta U = (f/2) n R Delta T.
Calculate final numerical value: Delta U = 3 * 8.314 * 100 = 2494.2 J.

solved_numericals.question: A rigid container holds 1 mole of a diatomic gas at temperature T_0. Due to electrical heating, heat Q is supplied to the gas, and 20% of this heat escapes through the container walls. Find the rise in temperature of the gas.
solution_steps: Net heat retained by the gas: Q_{net} = Q - 0.20 Q = 0.80 Q.
For a rigid container, volume is constant (dV = 0), so all retained heat goes into changing internal energy: Delta U = Q_{net} = 0.80 Q.
Relate internal energy change to temperature rise for a diatomic gas (f = 5, C_v = 5R/2): Delta U = n C_v Delta T = (5/2) R Delta T.
Equate and solve for Delta T: (5/2) R Delta T = 0.80 Q => Delta T =  rac{1.6 Q}{5 R} = 0.32  rac{Q}{R}.

solved_numericals.question: Using the van der Waals equation of state, find the change in internal energy when 1 mole of a real gas undergoes isothermal expansion from volume V_1 to V_2 at temperature T.
solution_steps: Start from the thermodynamic relation: (partial U / partial V)_T = T (partial P / partial T)_V - P.
Write the van der Waals equation: P =  rac{RT}{V-b} -  rac{a}{V^2}.
Calculate partial derivative (partial P / partial T)_V =  rac{R}{V-b}.
Substitute into the thermodynamic relation: (partial U / partial V)_T = T( rac{R}{V-b}) - ( rac{RT}{V-b} -  rac{a}{V^2}) =  rac{a}{V^2}.
Integrate with respect to volume from V_1 to V_2: Delta U = int_{V_1}^{V_2}  rac{a}{V^2} dV = a ( rac{1}{V_1} -  rac{1}{V_2}).

assumptions_and_limitations: Ideal gas internal energy formulations assume negligible intermolecular forces, which breaks down at high pressures and low temperatures.
Classical equipartition theorem fails at very low temperatures (cryogenic regimes) due to quantum freeze-out of vibrational and rotational degrees of freedom.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Internal energy depends on the path taken by the system during a thermodynamic process.
common_misconceptions.correct: Internal energy is a state function and depends only on the current thermodynamic state of the system.
common_misconceptions.why: Path dependence applies to path functions like heat (Q) and work (W), not state functions like internal energy (U).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Temperature is a measure of the total internal energy of a body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy per molecule, whereas internal energy is the total energy summed over all molecules.
common_misconceptions.why: A small cup of boiling water has a high temperature but lower total internal energy compared to a swimming pool full of lukewarm water.

common_misconceptions.wrong: For an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the internal energy changes because work is done.
common_misconceptions.correct: Internal energy remains constant during an isothermal process for an ideal gas.
common_misconceptions.why: Since temperature is constant, Delta T = 0 implies Delta U = 0; the heat absorbed is entirely converted into work.

quick_revision: Internal energy U is an extensive state function dependent solely on temperature for ideal gases.
For an ideal gas, U = (f/2) n R T.
In an isothermal process for an ideal gas, Delta U = 0.
In an adiabatic process, Delta U = -W.
For real gases, internal energy depends on both temperature and volume due to intermolecular potentials.
